Title: Providing hope for cancer patients
NewsSummary: AKU-SONAM alumna attends clinical trials at the University of Alabama Cancer Center
NewsContent:
Joyce Marete's passion for nursing began when she had to take care of her ailing grandfather just after she finished high school. Joyce would give him daily insulin injections as well as healthy food that was appropriate for a diabetic patient. At that point, she realized that she enjoyed providing care to those who needed it.

She has been a practising nurse for more than 15 years and currently works as an oncology and palliative care nurse at the Aga Khan University Hospital, Nairobi (AKUHN). While at the Aga Khan University School of Nursing and Midwifery (AKU-SONAM), she pursued oncology nursing as well as a Bachelor of Science in Nursing. More recently, Joyce was part of a team from the Hospital that travelled to the University of Alabama Birmingham (UAB) to learn more about the best practices when conducting clinical trials for cancer patients. The goal was to have her as part of a larger oncology team when a similar establishment is eventually developed at the Hospital.

From September 13 to October 5, 2019, AKU-SONAM alumna, Joyce Marete and three of her colleagues were at the University of Alabama Birmingham Cancer Centre, USA as part of an observership program.

The observership, called "UAB Phase I Clinical Trials Program" is a clinical research initiative dedicated to providing cancer patients with alternative treatment options. Essentially, this program involves enrolling willing cancer patients into clinical trials conducted by UAB Cancer Center staff and monitoring their progress while various treatment options are explored. According to a statement by the program's Director, Dr Mansoor Saleh in the Cancer Centre's newsletter, the program would be a "...close-to-home destination site for access to novel therapeutic options, thereby keeping patients close to friends and family."

Ms Marete and three other colleagues from the Aga Khan University Hospital Nairobi were there to observe the operations and processes involved in providing holistic cancer care to patients, to understand the structure of UAB's research team, observe how technology is deployed to conduct research as well as to appreciate how the different teams involved collaborated to achieve their objectives. The four were assigned mentors in their respective areas of expertise, who they shadowed for the duration of their visit. Ms Marete shadowed the clinical research coordinator and learned how patient care is delivered to the persons enrolled in clinical trials so as to adopt some of the best practices. This was a particularly vital visit as her team embarks on setting up an oncology clinical trial research unit led by Dr Saleh. On his part, Dr Saleh shared that "Before, clinical trials were just a dream. Today it is fair to say that clinical trials are in the horizon. We have the institutional support, the trained staff and the commitment to provide our patients in Kenya access to novel therapies as part of the UAB clinical trials program."

Joyce seems to have a soft spot for cancer patients. She shared that, "It is always a big challenge to see a young, newly-diagnosed advanced cancer patient, who is still in shock from the news of the illness and still has to deal with taking care of their young children. This is a common scenario." However, there is hope for cancer patients who interact with Joyce because she has invested in equipping herself with knowledge in oncology. She adds that "All the training I've received is to prepare me to be a competent and knowledgeable oncology nurse. I want to ensure that I can offer quality care to cancer patients."
